questions.question_text: What is the primary difference between perennial rivers and rain-fed seasonal rivers in India?
questions.correct_answer: Perennial rivers (like the Ganga or Yamuna) originate from high-altitude melting glaciers or permanent springs, maintaining year-round water flow, whereas seasonal rivers rely solely on monsoon rainfall and dry up significantly during summer.
questions.detailed_explanation:
HINT: Compare glacier/spring source water supply against seasonal monsoon dependency.

DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP REASONING:
Perennial rivers receive continuous water input from glacier melt during hot summer months and monsoon rain during wet seasons. Seasonal rivers lack glacier sources, flowing heavily only during monsoon rains.

questions.question_text: The flagship national initiative established to clean, restore, and rejuvenate the River Ganga ecosystem is called the _____ Gange programme.
questions.correct_answer: Namami
questions.detailed_explanation:
HINT: Comprehensive river conservation program launched by the Government of India.

DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP REASONING:
The Namami Gange programme integrates sewage treatment infrastructure, industrial effluent monitoring, riverfront development, and biodiversity conservation along the Ganga River.

questions.question_text: Why does removing tree vegetation and cutting forests along riverbanks increase the destructive power of seasonal river floods?
options: A) Tree roots bind riverbank soil and slow surface runoff momentum; removing trees causes rapid soil erosion and rapid flood surges.
B) Trees drink all the flood water so removing them makes rivers dry.
C) Trees attract lightning that stops river water.
D) Removing trees turns freshwater into ocean salt.
questions.correct_answer: A) Tree roots bind riverbank soil and slow surface runoff momentum; removing trees causes rapid soil erosion and rapid flood surges.
questions.detailed_explanation:
HINT: Vegetation provides root anchorage and surface hydraulic roughness.

DETAILED STEP-BY-STEP REASONING:
Riparian tree root systems mechanically anchor riverbank soil against hydraulic scour, while trunk and foliage friction slows floodwater velocity. Deforestation destabilizes riverbanks, triggering erosion and severe downstream flooding.
